title: Apologetics
description: The reasoned defense of the Christian faith. Students study the biblical basis and methods of apologetics (classical, evidential, presuppositional, cumulative case, Reformed epistemology), arguments for God's existence, the reliability of Scripture, the resurrection of Jesus, the problem of evil, science and faith, world religions, and cultural apologetics - learning from the early apologists (Justin, Tertullian, Origen, Augustine) and later thinkers (Anselm, Aquinas, Calvin, Hodge), and practicing gentle, respectful conversation.

quiz_bank.question: Present the cosmological argument from contingency in your own words.
quiz_bank.answer_key: Things in the world exist contingently (they might not have existed and depend on causes); an infinite chain of dependent causes explains nothing; so there must be a necessary being that exists of itself and causes all contingent things - which we call God.

quiz_bank.question: How might an apologist present the fine-tuning argument, and what objection must be answered?

quiz_bank.question: Explain the free will defense against the logical problem of evil.
quiz_bank.answer_key: It is possible that God has good reason to create free creatures capable of genuine love and moral goodness; such freedom entails the possibility of evil; so God and evil are not logically contradictory - defeating the claim of logical incompatibility.

quiz_bank.question: How does the cross shape a Christian response to evil?
quiz_bank.answer_key: God does not stand aloof but enters suffering in Christ, bearing sin and injustice, defeating evil through the cross and resurrection, and promising a new creation where evil ends - giving hope and grounds to trust God amid unanswered questions.
